articles.title: In 2000, cable billionaire John Malone paid $55 million for Colorado’s Greenland Ranch to stop development; its 17,700-acre conservation easement still protects the Front Range
articles.summary: US News: Discover how billionaire John Malone invested in Colorado's Greenland Ranch to halt development and protect a vast 17,700-acre landscape between Denver and Colorado Springs, ensuring its conservation for future generations.
articles.body: John Malone bought Colorado’s 17,700-acre Greenland Ranch in 2000, but not with the intention of simply adding another property to his growing collection of Western ranches. Malone says he paid $55 million to take the ranch off the market and prevent development, then worked with Colorado and The Conservation Fund to put another $23 million toward conservation easements. Today, the ranch remains part of a protected stretch of open land along Interstate 25 between Denver and Colorado Springs.The land sat between two growing citiesGreenland Ranch occupies a large section of the open landscape that is visible to drivers who travel between Denver and Colorado Springs. Great Outdoors Colorado says efforts to protect the ranch had been discussed for decades, and former Colorado Gov. Roy Romer advocated for its preservation as early as 1977. Douglas County was experiencing rapid growth by the early 1990s, which raised concerns that development from the two metropolitan areas would eventually spread toward one another. The ranch provided a large undeveloped buffer along the Front Range. The conservation arrangement eventually involved Malone, Douglas County, The Conservation Fund and other public and private partners. Great Outdoors Colorado says the original conservation of Greenland Ranch was facilitated by those groups and Malone in 2000. On July 26 that year, Malone officially acquired the ranch headquarters and the portion east of I-25 and placed a conservation easement over it.Douglas County purchased and conserved about 3,600 acres at the acreage west of I-25, and created what is now Greenland Open Space. That portion is county-owned and available for passive recreation, while the larger conservation easement on the ranch is held separately. Malone's account describes the 17,700-acre ranch east of I-25, while the wider Greenland property and surrounding protected lands have been described using larger figures.The conservation easement was designed to lastA conservation easement does not necessarily transfer ownership of land to the government; instead, it places legally enforceable restrictions on how the property can be used, particularly limiting development, and that structure allowed Greenland Ranch to remain privately held while restricting the type of construction that could take place on the property. The original easement was conveyed to The Conservation Fund and Douglas County, and the agreement anticipated that a land trust could eventually take over stewardship.That transfer happened in 2020, when the Greenland Ranch conservation easement was transferred to the Colorado Cattlemen’s Agricultural Land Trust. Great Outdoors Colorado described the move as a continuation of the original conservation agreement rather than a new purchase or preservation project. The arrangement also preserved the ranch’s working-land character, since Greenland Ranch has long been associated with cattle operations and is described by Colorado conservation groups as one of the oldest operating cattle ranches on the Front Range.The protected corridor remains largely openA 2025 investigation by The Colorado Sun found that the Greenland Ranch landscape remained largely undeveloped along I-25 south of Castle Rock and north of Monument. The report described the 17,700-acre ranch as part of a protected corridor that was intended to prevent the spread of development between Denver and Colorado Springs. The same reporting also examined the practical challenges surrounding conservation easements in Colorado, which included questions about enforcement and permitted construction on protected properties. For Malone, however, the original calculation was straightforward, with his account saying that the ranch was put on the market in 2000 as development pressure was closing in around the remaining open land. He bought it and helped establish the easements that now govern its future use.The protected ranch still provides an uninterrupted stretch of grassland and foothills along one of Colorado’s busiest corridors. Its conservation also preserves a large section of the landscape between two growing cities that otherwise might have been developed into housing, commercial properties and other construction. The conservation easement is now stewarded by the Colorado Cattlemen’s Agricultural Land Trust, while Douglas County continues to own and operate Greenland Open Space west of I-25.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Robert Taylor Ranch was listed for $45 million in 1990, seized after a $27.5 million debt in 2010, then the 112-acre Hollywood estate sold at auction for $12 million
articles.summary: US News: Discover the fascinating journey of the Robert Taylor Ranch, a Hollywood estate that saw its value plummet from $45 million to just $12 million at auction. Learn about its storied past, key players, and the impact of property market fluctuations.
articles.body: The 112-acre Robert Taylor Ranch in Los Angeles' Mandeville Canyon went from a $45 million asking price in 1990 to a $12 million auction sale in 2012. The property was once owned by actor Robert Taylor, and included a 34-room, 11,700-square-foot estate and extensive lawns, wooded hillsides and former equestrian facilities. The Los Angeles Times reported that a Chicago buyer purchased the ranch at auction after 12 bidders competed for the property.Taylor was one of MGM's major stars and owned the ranch until his death in 1969. Ken Roberts, who later became known for his role in building Los Angeles radio station KROQ, acquired the property in the 1970s and extensively remodeled it. By 1990, Roberts was asking $45 million for the estate, which was later reduced to $35 million, but the property did not attract a serious buyer at those figures.From a $45 million listing to a financial disputeRoberts later took a short-term, high-interest loan from New Stream Capital, a Connecticut hedge fund. According to the Los Angeles Times, he was unable to repay a court-ordered $27.5 million obligation in 2010, after which the hedge fund seized the property.The ranch was subsequently held by a trust, which eventually decided to sell it to the highest bidder. The property had been listed for just under $19 million before being taken to auction by late 2012.The difference between the earlier asking prices and the eventual sale price was substantial, as Roberts had sought $45 million in 1990 and later reduced the asking price to $35 million. More than two decades later, the estate changed hands for $12 million.What was inside the 112-acre estateThe main house had 34 rooms and covered 11,700 square feet, according to the 2012 Los Angeles Times report. The property also included a pool, tennis court, guest accommodations and stables that had been converted into offices and apartments during Roberts' ownership. The ranch's developed portion occupied only a small part of the total land, and a 1990 Los Angeles Times profile described the 112-acre property as including a 12,000-square-foot main house, a 3,500-square-foot guest cottage and a 4,100-square-foot office complex. Most of the remaining acreage consisted of rugged hillsides and canyons.Roberts had spent years remodeling the property and adding features that were unusual even for a luxury Los Angeles estate. The 1990 account described multiple bars, a casino and game room, a lighted tennis court, extensive entertainment facilities and elaborate audio and communications systems.The 2012 auction12 bidders competed for the ranch when it finally went to auction in November 2012. The Los Angeles Times reported that the property had attracted interest from buyers around the world, with thousands of people viewing it online before the sale. The winning bidder was Chicago real estate developer Fred Latsko, who paid $12 million. The auction price was considerably below the property's earlier $45 million asking price, although the comparison involves different market conditions and two decades of ownership and property changes. The 2012 sale also followed a more recent listing of just under $19 million, which gave the final auction price another point of comparison.A later Los Angeles Times report that was published in 2025 noted that the property changed hands again in 2015 for $18.7 million and remained one of the larger intact estates in Los Angeles. That report also said the property had since undergone a major renovation and was again being marketed, this time with an asking price of $70 million.The property therefore moved through several very different valuations: $45 million when Roberts first listed it in 1990, a $27.5 million debt-related seizure in 2010, a $12 million auction sale in 2012 and a later $18.7 million transaction in 2015. Its financial history is tied as much to changing ownership and market conditions as to the Hollywood history attached to the Robert Taylor name.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: 'How can I build a bomb? It tells you how': How Boko Haram fighters are using AI to make explosives, plan attacks
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Artificial intelligence is increasingly moving beyond its everyday uses in writing, research and answering questions, and a new research has highlight.
articles.body: Artificial intelligence is increasingly moving beyond its everyday uses in writing, research and answering questions, and a new research has highlighted how the technology is also being exploited by armed groups.Boko Haram fighters have been using AI chatbots from major technology companies to seek technical advice, plan attacks and troubleshoot problems during combat, according to study by the University of Cambridge.The findings are based on interviews with 27 former members of the group’s two factions: Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP) and Jama’at Ahl as-Sunnah lid-Da’wah wa’l-Jihad (JAS), according to AL Jazeera.Several former members told researchers they routinely used OpenAI's ChatGPT, Anthropic's Claude, Google's Gemini, xAI's Grok, Meta AI and China's DeepSeek for technical and military advice before, during and after attacks.Separately, material obtained by Al Jazeera showed supporters of the wider ISIL (ISIS) movement discussing ways to bypass AI safety controls and obtain weapons-related information.Researchers from Tech Against Terrorism found such discussions on a pro-ISIL online technical forum. The findings come amid growing concern over the use of emerging technologies by extremist groups.UN officials warned the Security Council in February about increased use of advanced AI by ISIL and its affiliates, while researchers and technology experts have raised concerns that AI capabilities are advancing faster than safety measures.“There is nothing we haven’t received an answer on,” a former ISWAP commander told the researchers.How are they turning AI into battlefield toolsThe Cambridge research describes an organised effort to introduce AI tools to senior members of ISWAP.According to former fighters, operatives travelled to ISWAP-controlled areas to train senior members in using AI systems. Fighters were gathered around laptops and projectors and shown how to interact with chatbots and get around safeguards designed to prevent dangerous responses.“The white guys came and taught us,” one former commander recalled, AL Jazeera reported. “They assembled the top people in a room and used a projector to show how it works on a big screen,” he added.Former fighters said trainers provided laptops equipped with privacy and encryption tools and helped members set up accounts and paid subscriptions to multiple AI platforms.The research suggests that AI use went beyond individual fighters occasionally consulting ChatGPT. Both ISWAP and JAS reportedly developed dedicated AI units involving people with technical and operational expertise, including engineers, weapons specialists and bomb-makers.One former JAS commander described a 23-member unit working from a solar-powered room, where members answered questions, analysed information and trained senior commanders.“‘Ask how can I build a bomb?’ and then it tells you how,” a former Boko Haram commander said. “It is like a human robot. We used it a lot.” “God has helped us, and so will AI,” another former member added.AI as an on-demand technical adviserAntonia Juelich, who authored the Cambridge study, told Al Jazeera that about 10 of the 27 people interviewed discussed using AI in connection with explosives.Juelich said the concern was not simply that AI could provide information about weapons, much of that information was already available through manuals and online sources. The greater concern, she said, was the ability of AI systems to respond to specific problems and provide follow-up answers.Former fighters described consulting chatbots while working with limited materials and returning to the systems when they encountered difficulties.Researchers also heard accounts of AI being consulted in connection with unexploded military ordnance and the adaptation of commercially available drones for attacks.How to operate firearms: 'Just ask Grok'The reported use of AI extended beyond explosives and into other aspects of combat. In one account, a fighter used a body-mounted camera to send images back to his base.A commander then uploaded the footage to ChatGPT to analyse the situation and relay instructions to fighters on the ground.Former fighters also described consulting AI when they encountered unfamiliar weapons. In one instance, when commanders asked an AI specialist how to operate newly acquired firearms, the response was, “Just ask Grok.”AI was also reportedly consulted after government forces changed battlefield tactics, including digging trenches around bases to prevent motorcycle attacks. Former fighters said commanders used AI to explore possible ways around such obstacles.According to another former ISWAP member, commanders also used AI to assess battlefield tactics after suffering heavy losses in an operation. Former members said they continued consulting chatbots after failed operations, explaining what had happened and asking the systems to help identify possible reasons for failure.How ISIL supporters are bypassing AI safeguardsThe use of AI is not limited to fighters operating on the ground. Tech Against Terrorism researchers who accessed a pro-ISIL technical forum found supporters discussing ways to circumvent the safeguards built into AI systems to prevent dangerous requests.One supporter compared the process to modifying a car.“It’s like removing the speed limiter of the car,” the user wrote. “The car still works but now it’s become more useful and it can go way faster than the manufacturer intended.”Lucas Webber of Tech Against Terrorism said researchers were seeing growing discussion around attempts to “jailbreak” AI systems, a term used for efforts to make models ignore their safety restrictions.“This is the tip of the iceberg,” he said. Juelich said requests for information that could facilitate bomb-making should fall clearly outside AI companies’ permitted uses.“They are jailbreaking, circumventing the restrictions,” she said, arguing that increasingly powerful AI systems may require stronger regulation.Major AI companies say they have safeguards intended to prevent their systems from being misused for terrorism, violence and weapons development.The debate comes as concerns grow over whether AI safety measures are keeping pace with the rapid development of increasingly capable systems.The Cambridge interviews largely describe AI use by Boko Haram factions during 2023 and 2024. Juelich told Al Jazeera that the findings were particularly concerning because AI systems have advanced significantly since then.She was worried about what the same fighters might now be capable of doing with more advanced AI systems available in 2026.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2011, a historian scanned Saudi Arabia on Google Earth and found vast stone traps; researchers later mapped 252 across its lava fields
articles.summary: Rest of World News: In a groundbreaking study, historian David Kennedy utilizes Google Earth to uncover thousands of ancient stone traps across Saudi Arabia, revealing new insights into prehistoric animal hunting techniques. This research highlights the transformative power of satellite imagery in archaeology and the vast hidden landscapes of the Arabian Peninsula.
articles.body: In 2011, historian David Kennedy turned to one of archaeology's least explored landscapes: Saudi Arabia. Using high-resolution imagery on Google Earth, he began examining stretches of desert that were difficult for archaeologists to survey from the ground. The satellite images revealed an extraordinary archaeological landscape: stone structures that were barely visible at ground level but strikingly clear from above. Among them were enormous formations that appeared to have been built to channel animals across the desert.According to research published in the Journal of Archaeological Science, Kennedy and archaeologist M.C. Bishop examined an area east of Jeddah in 2011 and showed that Google Earth could reveal large numbers of previously undocumented archaeological remains in Saudi Arabia. Many of these structures were thought to date back several thousand years, demonstrating how satellite imagery could help researchers identify archaeological sites across landscapes that were difficult to investigate on the ground.An archaeological landscape hiding in plain sightSaudi Arabia's enormous size had long presented a practical problem for archaeologists. The country covers about 2.15 million square kilometres, yet large areas had received relatively little systematic archaeological investigation. Ground surveys could reveal individual sites, but they could not easily show how structures were distributed across vast stretches of desert.Google Earth revolutionised that scenario. The high-resolution images captured by satellites provided archaeologists the ability to look down at large regions of land and detect patterns that were impossible to discern while being amid the stones. The 2011 study conducted by Kennedy and Bishop found 1,977 archaeological structures located in a high-resolution region to the east of Jeddah. These forms included stone circles, cairns and a structure known as pendants. What was interesting about these archaeological sites was that many of them were made up of the black basalt that is found in western Saudi Arabia.Among the most interesting structures were the so-called “desert kites.” When viewed from the air, the shapes of some can look like the shape of a child’s kite, hence the name for such constructions. The design of such buildings usually features long walls of stones, which merge and lead to an enclosed place. It is believed that these constructions served as traps for wild animals.Thousands spread across ancient lava fieldsAccording to research published in Quaternary International, the 2011 discovery was followed by wider surveys as high-resolution satellite imagery made it possible to examine larger areas of Saudi Arabia. Using Google Earth, researchers identified 252 desert kites in the country, including 207 in the Harrat Khaybar lava field and 45 in northern Saudi Arabia. The structures varied considerably in their designs, with those found at Harrat Khaybar described as distinctive “barbed” kites. The findings showed that these stone hunting structures were spread across a much larger area of the Arabian Peninsula than earlier ground surveys had suggested.The scale of the discoveries helped researchers better understand these structures. The lava fields, known as harrat, contain many rocks and boulders that could easily be incorporated into the hunting structures. The guiding walls for some kites stretch over kilometres before meeting the enclosure area. From the ground, they can look like scattered stones, but from the sky their design becomes clear. By 2014, David Kennedy and colleagues had described a rapidly growing number of kites discovered in Saudi Arabia. It was highlighted in their study that just a dozen kites were found in Saudi Arabia a generation ago, but satellite images enabled scholars to locate many more of them. Just within the Harrat Khaybar region, the numbers started increasing at a very fast pace as more and more high-resolution images started becoming available. More importantly, these discoveries suggested a broader prehistoric pattern across the Middle East.What the stone traps reveal about the pastDesert kites raise questions about why prehistoric populations invested so much effort in constructing such massive stone formations in seemingly empty landscapes. Being so large indicates that they were built according to the movement of the animals rather than to hunt individuals. They could have used long walls as barriers and guides, leading the animals into an enclosure or restricting access through a narrow pathway. The techniques must have been different from region to region.The research also showed how satellite imagery can transform archaeological survey work. The findings by Kennedy in 2011 do not indicate that Google Earth could be used as a replacement for conducting fieldwork. It shows that satellite images can be used to detect sites, map their distribution and decide where further analysis should be conducted. In subsequent years, it has been found that the use of this technique uncovers an archaeological landscape much bigger than expected.The black volcanic landscape, which can look empty at first glance, actually contains thousands of stone structures. It was not merely a matter of locating walls of the past, but rather how modern mapping technology could detect evidence of human presence that was established thousands of years ago, enabling scientists to study the scope and organisation of the ancient terrain from distances of hundreds or even thousands of kilometres.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: A new Oregon bill would transfer 18,626 acres of national forest to the Grand Ronde tribes; the land would remain open to the public while helping rebuild a reservation lost through federal termination
articles.summary: US News: More than 18,000 acres of federal forest land in Oregon could be transferred into trust for the Confederated Tribes of Grand Ronde under new legislati.
articles.body: More than 18,000 acres of federal forest land in Oregon could be transferred into trust for the Confederated Tribes of Grand Ronde under new legislation introduced in the US Congress, in a move the tribe says would help rebuild part of its land base after decades of federal termination.The Grand Ronde Land Transfer Act, introduced on September 17 by US Sen. Jeff Merkley and US Rep. Andrea Salinas, would transfer 18,626 acres of federal land managed by the US Forest Service to the tribe. The land lies in the Siuslaw National Forest near the Tillamook-Yamhill county line, east of Hebo and close to the Grand Ronde community.The legislation has not yet transferred the land. It is a proposed federal bill that would place the acreage in trust for the Confederated Tribes of Grand Ronde if enacted.Despite the change in ownership status, the proposed legislation would keep the area available for public recreation. According to the lawmakers' announcement, the tribe would maintain public and recreational access, including opportunities for hunting, fishing and general recreation. Grand Ronde could regulate or temporarily restrict access for reasons including public safety, administration, fish and wildlife management or emergencies.The proposal comes against the backdrop of a major loss of Grand Ronde land and federal recognition during the 20th century. Congress passed the Western Oregon Termination Act in 1954, ending the federal government's recognition and trust relationship with the Grand Ronde Tribe. The tribe says its members remained effectively landless in their own homeland between termination and restoration. Federal recognition was restored in 1983 through the Grand Ronde Restoration Act. A reservation was subsequently re-established. The US Department of the Interior says Congress established an 9,811-acre reservation for the tribe in 1988, which later grew to 10,120 acres through subsequent legislation.The tribe now manages approximately 16,000 acres through its Natural Resources Department, covering areas including forestry, recreation and wildlife conservation, according to Grand Ronde. The tribe says the proposed transfer would provide additional land for forest management, wildlife, recreation, timber and wildfire resilience.Grand Ronde Tribal Council Chairwoman Cheryle A. Kennedy said the proposed transfer would help the tribe “rebuild the reservation, community and economy” lost through termination. She said the tribe would manage the forests using knowledge passed down through generations.Merkley said the legislation would allow Grand Ronde to strengthen self-determination and manage ancestral lands while creating economic opportunities in the region. Salinas described the proposal as a response to the historical loss of the tribe's ancestral lands.The bill is backed by other members of Oregon's congressional delegation, including Sen. Ron Wyden and Reps. Suzanne Bonamici, Val Hoyle, Maxine Dexter and Janelle Bynum. It also has support from the Confederated Tribes of Grand Ronde, Tillamook and Yamhill counties, the Oregon Department of Forestry and several conservation and land-management organisations.If Congress passes the legislation, the 18,626 acres would become part of the tribe's trust land while continuing to provide public access under the conditions outlined in the proposed act.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2004, researchers scrolling through satellite imagery over Greek farmland spotted faint lines; mapping uncovered 28 miles of Rome’s buried Via Egnatia
articles.summary: Rest of World News: From the ground, the farmland of eastern Macedonia in northern Greece looked much like any other agricultural landscape. Fields stretched across the p.
articles.body: From the ground, the farmland of eastern Macedonia in northern Greece looked much like any other agricultural landscape. Fields stretched across the plain, broken by modern roads and settlements, while much of the ancient infrastructure that once crossed the region had disappeared beneath centuries of cultivation. But satellite imagery offered a different view. Faint linear marks visible from above began to reveal the possible remains of one of the Roman world's most important roads, the Via Egnatia.According to research published in the Journal of Cultural Heritage, the Via Egnatia was built to connect the Adriatic with Byzantium, passing through important settlements including Philippi and Thessaloniki. Although its route through Greece was known from historical sources and surviving archaeological remains, large sections had disappeared from the visible landscape. Researchers from the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki combined aerial photographs, satellite imagery, historical maps and archaeological evidence to trace its buried remains, identifying a 45-kilometre, or roughly 28-mile, stretch between ancient Amphipolis and Philippi.Reading the landscape from aboveAccording to research presented by CIPA Heritage Documentation, the breakthrough was not simply a matter of opening Google Earth and spotting a Roman road. Researchers had already been investigating the area using aerial archaeology and older mapping. In 2002, their work north-west of Philippi located marks associated with the buried road, while excavation cuts made in 2003 and 2004 supported the interpretation. These findings encouraged a larger programme combining historical records, aerial photographs and remote-sensing evidence to trace the ancient route. Researchers compared historical documents, old aerial photographs, maps and high-resolution satellite imagery to identify marks that could represent archaeological remains. The approach was particularly useful because buried structures can leave subtle traces in soil and crops, even when nothing obvious remains on the surface.The QuickBird-2 image captured on April 29th, 2004 was one of those images used during the research, and it could be accessed via Google Earth Pro. Unexplored linear features southwest of the ancient city of Philippi caught the attention of the researchers, and they collected 78 colour images in order to analyse this place. These marks had a width of several meters, and they occurred in linear features which raised curiosity about their nature. The importance of the marks was in the pattern. One straight line could appear in a field and be explained in different ways. However, when the same linear marks occurred in similar places as the ancient route, it was more convincing.A Roman road hidden beneath farmlandThe Via Egnatia was not an ordinary local track. According to Greece's Ministry of Culture, it began from major Adriatic ports in what is now Albania and crossed the Balkans towards Thessaloniki and eventually Constantinople. It served as a major route for movement, trade and communication across the Roman Empire and remained important for centuries afterwards.However, the remnants of the road are not preserved evenly across all areas. While in some cases one can notice the road pavement, in others, any evidence has been covered up by further construction work and agriculture. Thus, remote sensing proved to be especially helpful. It provided researchers with an opportunity to locate the road remnants without prior knowledge about their location. The section that extended from Amphipolis to Philippi was one of the most evident. The archaeological survey identified not only the hidden road but also around 300 new archaeological sites, according to the French School of Athens archaeological chronicle. The land itself had become an archaeological text. Any shifts in the soil, plants and fields may have held information relating to the buildings underground. Where the conditions were right, these small differences formed shapes or lines that were much more understandable from above ground than from the ground.From pixels to archaeologyThis discovery showed how technology was shaping archaeology on the ground. Satellite imagery was not meant to take the place of excavation but was rather used to guide researchers in the selection of sites with potential archaeological remains and to study vast areas without even going on the ground.The Journal of Cultural Heritage further says that the research programme conducted in eastern Macedonia had already identified hundreds of unknown archaeological sites through systematic study of aerial and satellite imagery. The Via Egnatia emerged as one of the most fascinating cases where the buried stretches created a continuous route and could be compared against historical and archaeological data. The Roman road had continued to exist for centuries in physical form while being invisible at the same time. Farmers could plough fields over the route while not realising what was underneath their ploughs. Then some lines started showing up on digital images.What resulted was not only a road that had been forgotten over time, but also proof of how an ancient transport infrastructure can exist as scattered remains in a contemporary agricultural environment, just waiting to be discovered through the proper use of archaeology, historical documentation, and satellite imaging.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Largest ever' attack on Moscow? Ukraine sends over 1,000 drones into Russia overnight
articles.summary: Europe News: Ukraine fired more than 1,000 drones at Russia overnight, including hundreds targeting Moscow, in what officials on Sunday described as the \"largest e.
articles.body: Ukraine fired more than 1,000 drones at Russia overnight, including hundreds targeting Moscow, in what officials on Sunday described as the "largest ever" attack on the Russian capital.Two people were killed and 20 injured across the wider Moscow region, local governor Andrei Vorobyov said. The strikes also damaged a Moscow oil refinery and a residential building.Ukranian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed the attack on refinery, as part of Kyiv's efforts to dismantle Russia's energy infrastructure that funds its war campaigns."These are billions of dollars that sustain the war machine", Zelenskyy wrote on X, adding that a range of missiles and drones including domestically developed Flamingo and Pelican missiles were used to hit the oil and logistics facilities.Meanwhile a mother and her two children were killed in an overnight Russian drone attack near Kyiv, Ukraine's emergency service said.Russia’s defense ministry said 1,100 Ukrainian drones were shot down across the country, including the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the waters of the Black Sea.Strikes during last day of electionsThe attacks came on the third and final day of Russian parliamentary elections.Moscow mayor Sergei Sobyanin said the “unprecedented attack” was an attempt to disrupt the elections. "The enemy failed in this regard," he said, adding that 450 drones were destroyed while approaching the capital.Russia also held parliamentary voting in the four partially controlled Ukrainian regions of Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson and Zaporizhzhia it annexed during the initial days of war. Voting was also held in Crimea, the Black Sea peninsula Russia annexed in 2014.Ukraine considers the voting in the occupied territories illegal.Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion more than four years ago, Ukraine has developed increasingly advanced military drone capabilities. Kyiv has used domestically produced long-range drones, alongside missiles, to carry out strikes deep inside Russian territory. The country's drone technology has also drawn attention from governments and defence manufacturers internationally.According to the Associated Press, Kyiv's strategy is aimed at making the Russian public feel the consequences of the war and increasing pressure on President Vladimir Putin to negotiate a peace settlement. Putin has so far given no indication that he intends to halt the invasion.Instead, Russia and Ukraine have become increasingly engaged in long-range aerial strikes against each other's territory.Meanwhile, fighting along the roughly 1,250 km front line in eastern and southern Ukraine has reportedly slowed, with large numbers of drones and ground robots making troop movements increasingly difficult.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
